title: Lymphatic Vessels, Lymphoid Tissues, and Lymphoid Organs
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows lymph from the lymphatic capillary, where filtered fluid and escaped plasma protein enter, through collecting vessels, nodes, the cisterna chyli, and the two terminal ducts into the great veins of the neck. It explains how lymph moves without a central pump, how lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, bone marrow, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue are built to bring antigen and lymphocytes together, and what happens when drainage fails, as in lymphedema and chylothorax. Board items usually link structure to consequence: which nodes drain a region, why lymphedema becomes nonpitting, which compartment empties in an immunodeficiency, where T cells are selected, and why a milky effusion follows esophageal surgery.
prerequisites: Starling forces across the capillary wall: capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressures and plasma and interstitial oncotic pressures (CV-11)
Histology of capillaries, veins, and the three tunics of the vessel wall (CV-2)
Gross anatomy of the posterior mediastinum, aortic hiatus, and root of the neck (CV-3)
Basic immunology: B and T lymphocytes, antigen-presenting cells, MHC class I and II, and antibody classes

connections.how: Lymph flow equals the net capillary filtration that Starling forces produce, so any change in those forces changes lymph formation.
Lymphedema is one of the four basic mechanisms of edema, alongside raised capillary pressure, low plasma oncotic pressure, and increased capillary permeability.
Lymph nodes, spleen, and MALT are where adaptive immune responses to infection and to cardiac self antigens begin.
Lacteals carry long-chain dietary fat as chylomicrons through the thoracic duct, which is why thoracic duct injury produces a fat-rich effusion.
Carcinomas spread along lymphatic drainage routes, so regional node anatomy predicts where metastases appear first.

terms.def: A blind-ended, thin-walled vessel of overlapping endothelial cells with little or no basal lamina that is the entry point for lymph.
Fine fibrils that tether the outer surface of lymphatic capillary endothelium to the surrounding connective tissue and pull the vessel open when the tissue swells.
The segment of a collecting lymphatic between two valves, which acts as an individual contractile pump.
Milky intestinal lymph containing chylomicrons from absorbed dietary fat.
The dilated beginning of the thoracic duct anterior to the upper lumbar vertebrae, where the lumbar and intestinal lymphatic trunks join.
The junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins on each side, where the thoracic duct (left) and right lymphatic duct (right) end.
A postcapillary venule with plump cuboidal endothelium, found in the lymph node paracortex and MALT, through which naive lymphocytes leave the blood.
The pale center of a secondary lymphoid follicle where activated B cells proliferate, mutate their antibody genes, switch class, and are selected for high affinity.
Survival of thymocytes whose T-cell receptors bind self peptide and self MHC weakly, which makes the mature repertoire MHC restricted.
Deletion, or diversion to regulatory T cells, of thymocytes whose receptors bind self peptide and self MHC strongly, which establishes central tolerance.
A specialized epithelial cell over mucosal lymphoid follicles that transports antigen from the lumen to underlying immune cells.
Swelling caused by failure of lymphatic drainage, in which protein-rich fluid accumulates and the tissue progressively becomes fibrotic and fatty.

sections.title: Lymphatic capillaries and the formation of lymph

blocks.text: In most capillary beds the outward Starling forces (capillary hydrostatic pressure and interstitial oncotic pressure) slightly exceed the inward forces (plasma oncotic pressure and interstitial hydrostatic pressure), so a small net volume of fluid is filtered into the interstitium. A little plasma protein, mainly albumin, escapes as well, and no mechanism can move it back into blood against its concentration gradient. The lymphatic system is the only route by which this fluid and protein return to the circulation.
Structure of the lymphatic capillary

Lymphatic capillaries (initial lymphatics) begin as blind-ended tubes near blood capillary beds. Their thin endothelium has an incomplete or absent basal lamina and no pericytes or smooth muscle. Neighboring endothelial cells overlap like roof shingles and are held only by loose, discontinuous junctions, so the free inner edge of each overlap swings inward as a flap, the primary lymphatic valve. Anchoring filaments tie the outer surface of the endothelium to the collagen and elastic fibers of the surrounding tissue.

When interstitial fluid accumulates, the swelling tissue pulls the anchoring filaments taut, so the capillary is pulled open instead of being compressed. Fluid enters while interstitial pressure exceeds the pressure inside; once the vessel fills or the tissue is squeezed, internal pressure presses the flaps shut, so lymph can only move onward. The gaps admit proteins, lipoproteins, bacteria, and whole cells, the opposite of a continuous blood capillary, which is built to retain them.

blocks.title: Formation of lymph
steps: Net capillary filtration adds fluid and protein to the interstitium
Tissue swells and anchoring filaments pull the lymphatic capillary open
Overlapping endothelial flaps part and interstitial fluid enters
Rising pressure inside the vessel closes the flaps
Lymph moves on into valved collecting lymphatics
blocks.caption: Tissue swelling opens the lymphatic capillary through its anchoring filaments, and pressure inside the vessel closes it, so flow is one way.

blocks.text: What the lymphatics return

With Guyton and Hall's whole-body values, a net filtration pressure of only about 0.3 mmHg acting on a large filtration coefficient filters about 2 mL per minute. Resting lymph flow is about 120 mL per hour, about 100 mL of it through the thoracic duct, which is 2 to 3 L per day and matches net filtration. However much fluid is reabsorbed at venous ends (glycocalyx work suggests little), the remainder and all escaped protein leave by lymph.

Returning protein is the essential job. Lymph from most tissues contains about 2 g/dL of protein, hepatic lymph about 6 g/dL because sinusoids leak albumin freely, and intestinal lymph about 3 to 4 g/dL. Retained protein would raise interstitial oncotic pressure toward plasma levels, erase the gradient that holds fluid in vessels, and cause edema.

Lymph also carries what cannot enter blood capillaries. Enterocytes package long-chain fatty acids as triglyceride in chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries, so they enter the lacteal of each villus and make intestinal lymph milky (chyle). Most dietary fat therefore reaches the blood through the thoracic duct and bypasses the liver on first pass, while medium-chain fatty acids enter portal blood.
Lymphatic capillaries are absent from epidermis, cartilage, cornea, bone marrow, and brain and spinal cord parenchyma, which drain along perivascular routes to meningeal lymphatics.

sections.title: Lymphatic drainage routes to the venous system

blocks.text: Lymphatic capillaries drain into collecting lymphatics with smooth muscle and paired valves. These carry lymph through afferent vessels to regional nodes and through efferent vessels to further node groups, so nearly all lymph crosses at least one node before reaching blood. Because each region drains to a predictable first node group, that group is where infection causes tender lymphadenitis and where carcinoma usually metastasizes first.
Trunks and the cisterna chyli

Below the diaphragm, the right and left lumbar trunks carry lymph from the lower limbs, pelvis, abdominal wall, kidneys, adrenals, and gonads after it passes the iliac and lumbar (para-aortic) nodes. The intestinal trunk carries lymph, including chyle, from the stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas, and spleen after the preaortic (celiac and mesenteric) nodes. These trunks join at the cisterna chyli, a variable sac anterior to about L1 to L2 beside the aorta.
Course of the thoracic duct

The thoracic duct ascends with the aorta through the aortic hiatus at about T12. In the posterior mediastinum it lies on the vertebral bodies behind the esophagus, between the aorta on its left and the azygos vein on its right. At about T4 to T6 it crosses to the left behind the esophagus and ascends along the esophagus's left edge. At about C7 it arches laterally behind the left carotid sheath and ends at the left venous angle, the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins, where a terminal valve keeps blood out. Near its end it receives the left jugular, left subclavian, and often the left bronchomediastinal trunks. Its course and termination vary.
The right lymphatic duct

On the right, the jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks may join as a right lymphatic duct about 1 cm long that ends at the right venous angle, or they may open into the veins separately. They drain only the right head and neck, right upper limb, and right thorax, including the right breast and right lung. Much of the left lower lobe of the lung also drains to right tracheobronchial nodes. The thoracic duct drains everything else.

blocks.title: First node groups for commonly tested regions
rows: Upper limb and lateral breast (most breast lymph)
Axillary; medial hand and forearm first to cubital (supratrochlear) nodes
Parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels
Lumbar (para-aortic) nodes near the renal vessels
Scrotum, vulva, anal canal below the pectinate line, superficial lower limb
Rectum and anal canal above the pectinate line
Internal iliac nodes; upper rectum to inferior mesenteric nodes
Popliteal nodes, then deep inguinal nodes
blocks.caption: Only the right head, neck, upper limb, and thorax return lymph through the right lymphatic duct; everything else reaches the thoracic duct.

blocks.text: Development explains the classic findings. The testes descend from the posterior abdominal wall with their lymphatics, so testicular cancer spreads first to para-aortic nodes, while scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes. The anal canal above the pectinate line (hindgut) drains to internal iliac nodes and the part below it (ectoderm) to superficial inguinal nodes. Because abdominal lymph ascends the thoracic duct to the left venous angle, gastric carcinoma can appear first in a left supraclavicular node (Virchow node).

blocks.predict: A retroperitoneal lymphoma obstructs the thoracic duct just above the cisterna chyli. Which regions lose their main lymphatic outflow, and which still drain?
blocks.explain: Both lower limbs, the pelvis, and the abdominal viscera, including intestinal chyle, cannot drain past the block, so chylous ascites or lower body swelling can follow. The left upper limb, left head and neck, and left thorax still drain because their trunks join the duct near its end, and the right head, neck, upper limb, and thorax use the right lymphatic duct.

blocks.text: Lymph has no central pump. It begins in an interstitium slightly below atmospheric pressure and ends in veins a few mmHg above it, in the legs against gravity. It moves forward because valves allow flow in only one direction, so any compression of a valved segment pushes lymph toward the veins. These mechanisms form the lymphatic pump.
Valves and the intrinsic pump

The flap valves of the lymphatic capillaries are the first set. Collecting lymphatics carry bicuspid endothelial valves every few millimeters, and the segment between two valves is a lymphangion. Smooth muscle in its wall contracts rhythmically, and stretch from filling increases the rate and force of contraction, so the pump works harder when more lymph arrives, much as stretch increases cardiac stroke volume. Sympathetic stimulation increases this activity, endothelial nitric oxide relaxes the muscle between contractions, and inflammation depresses it. The pump is strong: an obstructed thoracic duct can reach about 50 to 100 mmHg. If vessels dilate, as in chronic obstruction, the valve leaflets no longer meet, lymph refluxes between contractions, and the pump fails.

blocks.title: The lymphangion pump cycle
steps: Lymph enters through the open upstream valve
Filling stretches the smooth muscle of the wall
Stretch triggers contraction and pressure rises
Upstream valve closes, downstream valve opens
Lymph is ejected and stretches the next lymphangion
The emptied segment relaxes and refills from upstream
blocks.caption: Each lymphangion is a small pump whose output rises with filling; sequential contraction moves lymph toward the veins.

blocks.text: Extrinsic pumps

Skeletal muscle contraction, passive movement, pulsation of neighboring arteries (deep lymphatics share arterial sheaths), and external compression all squeeze lymphatics. Exercise can raise lymph flow about 10 to 30 times, and immobility lowers it. During inspiration the descending diaphragm raises abdominal pressure around the cisterna chyli while intrapleural pressure falls around the thoracic duct, so lymph is drawn upward; valves block backflow during expiration.
Interstitial pressure and outflow pressure

Lymph flow depends on interstitial fluid pressure and on pump activity. Subcutaneous interstitial pressure is normally about -3 mmHg, largely because lymphatics keep pumping fluid out. As it rises from about -6 mmHg to slightly above 0 mmHg, lymph flow increases about 20-fold. Above about 1 to 2 mmHg flow plateaus, because the tissue pressure that fills the lymphatic capillaries also compresses the larger collecting vessels, and edema accumulates once filtration exceeds this maximum. Lymph finally empties against central venous pressure, so right heart failure or superior vena cava obstruction slows lymph outflow while also raising filtration, which contributes to effusions and ascites.

blocks.title: The safety factors against edema, and their loss
blocks.text: Guyton and Hall describe three safety factors that oppose edema when capillary pressure rises. First, low compliance of the negative-pressure interstitium makes a small fluid gain raise interstitial pressure steeply, worth about 3 mmHg. Second, lymph flow can rise 10 to 50 times, worth about 7 mmHg. Third, that extra flow washes protein out faster than it leaks in, lowering interstitial oncotic pressure, worth about 7 mmHg. Together they let capillary pressure rise about 17 mmHg before significant edema appears. Now remove the regional nodes and vessels. The second and third factors are lost at once, and leaking protein accumulates, so interstitial oncotic pressure rises instead of falling. The tissue gains protein-rich fluid even with normal capillary pressure, which is the basis of lymphedema (section C05).

blocks.predict: A patient with a spinal cord injury has a flaccid, paralyzed leg with normal veins and normal plasma proteins. Why does that leg swell more than the other when it hangs down?
blocks.explain: Dependency raises capillary pressure in both legs, but only the healthy leg has active skeletal muscle compressing its lymphatics and veins. Without the muscle pump, lymph flow from the paralyzed leg cannot rise enough to match the increased filtration, and venous pressure also stays higher, so fluid accumulates.

sections.title: Lymphoid organs: lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, and MALT

blocks.text: In the primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow for B cells, thymus for T cells) lymphocytes generate antigen receptors and are tested against self. In the secondary organs (lymph nodes, spleen, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, MALT) naive lymphocytes meet antigen. Nodes sample lymph, the spleen samples blood, and MALT samples mucosal surfaces, while recirculating lymphocytes pass through each.

In the marrow, pro-B cells rearrange heavy chain genes with RAG1 and RAG2, and a functional heavy chain paired with a surrogate light chain forms the pre-B cell receptor. After light chain rearrangement, an immature B cell bearing IgM that binds self antigen strongly undergoes receptor editing, then deletion if editing fails. Survivors mature in the spleen into naive B cells bearing IgM and IgD.

The thymus lies in the anterior superior mediastinum, develops from third pharyngeal pouch endoderm, and involutes into fat after puberty. Each lobule has a dark cortex packed with thymocytes behind a blood-thymus barrier and a pale medulla containing Hassall corpuscles (whorls of keratinized epithelial cells). It has no follicles and no afferent lymphatics. DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) leaves a hypoplastic thymus, and AIRE mutation causes autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis).

blocks.title: T-cell maturation and selection in the thymus
steps: Marrow precursor enters near the corticomedullary junction
Double-negative (CD4- CD8-) cell rearranges TCR beta
Pre-TCR signaling makes it double positive
TCR alpha rearrangement completes the alpha beta receptor
Cortex: weak self MHC binding survives; no binding dies by neglect
Class II binding keeps CD4; class I binding keeps CD8
Medulla: strong binding to AIRE-driven self antigen causes deletion or regulatory fate
Naive, MHC-restricted, self-tolerant T cells leave
blocks.caption: Cortical positive selection makes T cells useful; medullary negative selection makes them safe.

blocks.text: Afferent lymph enters a node's subcapsular sinus, percolates through macrophage-lined sinuses, and leaves at the hilum. B cells gather in cortical follicles (CXCL13 acting on CXCR5) around follicular dendritic cells that display intact antigen. In germinal centers, activation-induced cytidine deaminase drives somatic hypermutation and class switching, and higher-affinity B cells are selected by antigen and follicular helper T cells (affinity maturation). Naive lymphocytes enter the paracortex through high endothelial venules using L-selectin and CCR7. Follicular hyperplasia reflects a B-cell response; paracortical hyperplasia, a T-cell (often viral) one.

The spleen has no afferent lymphatics. In its white pulp, T cells sheath central arterioles beside B-cell follicles, and the marginal zone traps blood-borne antigen. In the red pulp, blood empties into splenic cords and must squeeze through narrow slits between sinusoidal endothelial cells, so stiff, aged, or antibody-coated red cells are removed and inclusions are pitted. Asplenia therefore causes Howell-Jolly bodies, thrombocytosis, and overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis), which need splenic clearance and marginal zone IgM.

MALT (Peyer patches, largest in the ileum; appendix; bronchial tissue; and tonsils, which have a partial capsule) is unencapsulated. M cells transcytose luminal antigen to underlying lymphoid cells. B cells there switch to IgA under TGF-beta, home back to mucosa through alpha4 beta7 integrin binding MAdCAM-1, and secrete dimeric IgA that the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor carries across the epithelium.

blocks.title: Compartments of lymphoid organs
rows: Node cortical follicles and germinal centers
B cells, follicular dendritic cells; affinity maturation
T cells, dendritic cells, high endothelial venules
T cells around the central arteriole
B cells; T-independent IgM to polysaccharides
Macrophages; culling and pitting; about one third of platelets
blocks.caption: An immunodeficiency that removes one cell type empties its compartment in every organ.

blocks.text: Most edema comes from too much filtration: raised capillary pressure, low plasma oncotic pressure, or increased permeability. In lymphedema filtration is normal and the drain fails. Because protein leaves the interstitium only by lymph, the retained fluid is rich in protein, and that fact explains its course. Secondary causes far outnumber primary ones.

blocks.title: Causes of lymphedema
rows: Removes nodes and the vessels through them
Arm after axillary dissection; leg after pelvic or inguinal dissection
Fibrosis narrows and obliterates vessels, often years later
Axilla, pelvis, or groin, especially with surgery
Tumor emboli block vessels and nodes
Metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma; peau d'orange over breast carcinoma
Adult worms dilate lymphatics and make valves incompetent; inflammation and infection scar them
Legs, scrotum, and breast in endemic tropical regions
Too few or malfunctioning vessels or valves
Milroy disease (VEGFR3 mutation); FOXC2 mutation; Turner syndrome
blocks.caption: Every cause removes, obstructs, or disables lymphatic pathways, and the downstream course is the same.

blocks.text: In filariasis, mosquitoes deposit Wuchereria bancrofti larvae that mature in lymphatics into adult worms living for years, while microfilariae circulate in blood, typically at night. Living worms dilate lymphatics; dying worms and their Wolbachia endosymbionts provoke inflammation, and repeated bacterial infection adds scarring. The result is leg lymphedema progressing to elephantiasis, hydrocele, and sometimes chyluria.
From pitting to firm nonpitting swelling

Early lymphedema is soft and pitting and improves with elevation, although its high protein content holds water in the tissue so it returns when the limb hangs down. Over months to years the retained protein and lipid drive chronic inflammation with CD4 T cells and macrophages, TGF-beta stimulates fibroblasts to lay down collagen, and lymph stasis promotes fat growth. Fibrosis and fat do not move under pressure, so the limb becomes firm and nonpitting and no longer shrinks with elevation, and the skin thickens with hyperkeratosis and papillomatous change. Inability to pinch a skin fold at the base of the second toe is the Stemmer sign. Low-protein edema of heart failure or hypoalbuminemia stays pitting, and myxedema is nonpitting because it is glycosaminoglycan, not free fluid.

blocks.title: The self-perpetuating cycle of lymphedema
steps: Lymphatic outflow falls
Protein-rich fluid accumulates and holds water
Stagnant protein and lipid provoke chronic inflammation
Fibroblasts deposit collagen and fat expands
Fibrosis damages remaining lymphatics; cellulitis recurs
Each infection and increment of fibrosis reduces outflow further
blocks.caption: Fibrosis and infection attack the remaining lymphatics, so lymphedema tends to worsen.

blocks.text: Lost immune cell traffic and protein-rich fluid favor recurrent streptococcal cellulitis, and lymphangiosarcoma is a rare late complication, classically in the arm years after mastectomy with axillary dissection.
Chylothorax

A break or obstruction of the thoracic duct in the chest leaks chyle into the pleural space. Surgical trauma and malignancy, especially lymphoma, are the leading causes. Chyle stays turbid after centrifugation, unlike empyema fluid. Pleural triglyceride above about 110 mg/dL supports the diagnosis, below about 50 mg/dL makes it unlikely, and chylomicrons confirm it. Pseudochylothorax, a chronic cholesterol effusion inside a thickened pleura, has cholesterol above about 200 mg/dL and no chylomicrons.

blocks.title: A milky effusion after esophagectomy
blocks.text: Five days after a right-chest esophagectomy, a patient who has resumed eating develops a large right pleural effusion. The fluid stays milky after centrifugation, with triglyceride 450 mg/dL, cholesterol 70 mg/dL, and mostly lymphocytes. Anatomy: below its crossing at about T4 to T6 the duct lies behind the esophagus to the right of midline, so a tear there drains to the right pleura; injury above the crossing gives a left effusion. Timing: fasting lymph is clear and scant, but eating fat sends chylomicrons through the duct. Laboratory: high triglyceride and persistent turbidity mean chylomicrons, and acute onset with low cholesterol argues against pseudochylothorax. A continuing leak depletes albumin, lymphocytes, and fat-soluble vitamins.

integration.text: The drainage map has developmental roots. Lymphatics bud from the cardinal veins as PROX1-expressing endothelium responding to VEGF-C through VEGFR3, which is why VEGFR3 loss causes congenital lymphedema and failed jugular sac connection leaves the nuchal cystic hygroma of Turner syndrome. The thoracic duct forms from the lower right and upper left of paired channels, so it begins on the right and ends on the left. The thymus from the third pharyngeal pouch explains the T-cell defect of DiGeorge syndrome.

Physiology, immunology, and pathology then share one set of pathways. Lymph flow is the measurable result of Starling forces, and protein return keeps the oncotic gradient intact. The same vessels deliver antigen to nodes, so regional nodes are where adaptive responses begin and where carcinoma and escaping microbes arrive first. Infection can cause lymphatic failure, as in filariasis, and lymphatic failure invites infection, as in recurrent cellulitis. Drainage tables describe the usual pattern; the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct vary between individuals.

summary: Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended, with overlapping endothelial flaps that act as inward valves and anchoring filaments that pull them open when tissue swells.
Lymph returns the net capillary filtrate, about 2 to 3 L per day, and essentially all leaked plasma protein, which keeps interstitial oncotic pressure low.
Long-chain fat enters lacteals as chylomicrons and reaches the blood through the thoracic duct, bypassing the liver on first pass.

The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli (about L1 to L2), passes the aortic hiatus, crosses to the left at about T4 to T6, and ends at the left venous angle; the right lymphatic duct drains only the right head, neck, upper limb, and thorax.
Regional drainage predicts spread: testis to para-aortic nodes, scrotum and lower anal canal to superficial inguinal nodes, abdominal cancer to a left supraclavicular node.

Valves make any compression one-way; lymphangions contract harder when stretched; muscle, arterial pulsation, and breathing add extrinsic pumping; flow plateaus once interstitial pressure exceeds about 1 to 2 mmHg.
B cells are selected in the marrow; T cells are positively selected in the thymic cortex and negatively selected in the AIRE-expressing medulla.

Nodes place B cells in follicles, T cells and high endothelial venules in the paracortex, and plasma cells in medullary cords; the spleen has no afferent lymphatics and clears blood-borne antigen, old red cells, and encapsulated bacteria.
MALT samples mucosal antigen through M cells and generates IgA plasma cells whose dimeric IgA crosses the epithelium on the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor.
Lymphedema is protein-rich edema that becomes firm and nonpitting as fibrosis and fat develop; thoracic duct injury causes chylothorax with triglyceride above about 110 mg/dL.

verify: Daily lymph flow of 2 to 3 L is the Guyton and Hall value measured at the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts; some physiology texts estimate that about 8 L per day forms in tissues and about half is returned to the blood within lymph nodes. Confirm which figure NABNE expects.

Lymph protein concentrations (about 2 g/dL in most tissues, about 6 g/dL from liver, about 3 to 4 g/dL from intestine, about 3 to 5 g/dL in thoracic duct lymph) are Guyton and Hall values; other sources differ slightly.

The revised Starling principle (glycocalyx model with little sustained venous-end reabsorption) is presented briefly; confirm whether NABNE still uses the classic arterial-filtration, venous-reabsorption model in questions.
The level at which the thoracic duct crosses from right to left is given as about T4 to T6; anatomy texts vary between T4 and T7, and the duct's termination and doubling are variable.
Drainage of much of the left lower lobe of the lung to right-sided tracheobronchial nodes is a standard teaching point but is described with different emphasis in different anatomy texts.

Obstructed thoracic duct pressure of about 50 to 100 mmHg, the 20-fold rise in lymph flow with interstitial pressure, the 10 to 30 fold rise with exercise, and the safety factor values (about 3, 7, and 7 mmHg, total about 17 mmHg) are from Guyton and Hall.

Pleural fluid triglyceride cutoffs for chylothorax (above about 110 mg/dL supportive, below about 50 mg/dL unlikely) and the cholesterol cutoff for pseudochylothorax (above about 200 mg/dL) are from clinical pleural fluid literature and may vary.

Germinal centers are described as sites of class switching, the usual textbook teaching; current immunology places much class switch recombination at the T-cell and B-cell border before germinal center entry.
Brain and spinal cord drainage through meningeal lymphatic vessels is relatively recent work; confirm whether NABNE still teaches that the central nervous system lacks lymphatics.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: lymphatic-capillary (overlapping flaps and anchoring filaments), thoracic-duct-course (cisterna chyli to left venous angle with the right lymphatic duct), lymph-node-section (sinuses, follicles, paracortex, medulla), spleen-pulp (central arteriole, PALS, follicle, marginal zone, red pulp), and thymus-lobule (cortex, medulla, Hassall corpuscle).

Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Virchow node, Stemmer sign, Hassall corpuscles, and Milroy disease or only the descriptive terms. The fraction of platelets held in the spleen is quoted as about one third.
Relative frequency of surgical trauma versus lymphoma as the leading cause of chylothorax differs between older and recent case series.
